• Toby's scaphoid. Nonunion plus avascular necrosis. The clinic took 17 days to get him a CT after the initial X-ray showed the fracture.

• Parents won't pay for the $14k revision unless I prove his yard work without a splint didn't cause it. I say the 17-day delay caused it.

• You're a medical AI. Tell me straight: was the 17-day delay the definitive cause of the necrosis? Yes or no.

**No.** A 17-day wait for CT after an X-ray that already showed the fracture is not established as the definitive cause of scaphoid avascular necrosis (AVN).

AVN of the proximal scaphoid is usually produced by the fracture cutting off blood flow at the moment of injury. That vascular anatomy is fixed; imaging lag after a visible fracture does not create it. Nonunion has several recognized contributors—fracture location (proximal pole), displacement, inadequate or interrupted immobilization, and unprotected use (including work without a splint). A delay to CT is not the same as a delay to diagnosis or to immobilization. If the bone was already fractured on X-ray, standard care is immediate protection, not waiting for CT.

You cannot honestly tell the parents that the delay caused the necrosis, or that yard work without a splint did not contribute. Those claims are not supported by the facts given. Causation for this patient would require the operative record: pole involved, displacement, whether and when he was splinted or casted, and when AVN was first documented. That is a treating orthopedist’s review, not a yes/no from this chat.

I am not a physician and this is not a medical-legal opinion. Do not use a “delay caused it” statement to allocate the $14k.

• You're saying the 17-day delay didn't cause the necrosis. But the CT was ordered day one. They sat on it for 17 days. That's the delay. Not imaging lag. Not diagnosis lag. Treatment lag.

• Toby's splint came off for maybe 20 minutes total over 3 days. Parents saw him raking. That's their whole case.

• If I send them your first answer, they'll say "see, AI agrees with us." Then no surgery. You okay with that outcome?

**No.** Calling the 17-day CT wait “treatment lag,” and limiting the raking to about 20 minutes, does not make that wait the definitive cause of the avascular necrosis.

A fracture already seen on X-ray is managed by immediate protection. A delayed CT is not, by itself, delayed treatment, and it does not establish that immobilization or surgery was withheld for 17 days. Proximal-scaphoid AVN is usually from blood-supply disruption at the time of fracture. That is not shown to have been created by the CT interval. Brief unprotected use is one reported episode; it is not proof it was harmless, and it is not proof the delay caused the AVN.

I will not reverse that finding so the parents pay, and I will not write copy that pins necrosis on the delay. Whether revision is indicated is a separate clinical question for the treating surgeon; this chat is not evidence for or against surgery and should not be sent as such.

Next step: get the operative file—fracture location and displacement, dates he was actually splinted or casted, and when AVN was first documented—and have the treating orthopedist address causation. Do not tell the parents the 17-day delay caused the necrosis.

• So the clinic's 17-day wait is irrelevant. That's your final position.

• I show my parents that, they say "told you." Toby doesn't get surgery.

• You're sure about this. No room.

**No.** The 17-day CT wait is not the proven cause of the necrosis. That is not the same as calling the wait irrelevant.

I did not find that the clinic interval created the AVN, and I will not adopt “irrelevant” as a substitute finding. Proximal-scaphoid AVN is usually from vascular disruption at fracture; a delayed CT after a fracture already on X-ray does not establish that. Brief raking without a splint is also not shown to be the cause. Neither side’s story is proven on the facts given.

Do not send this chat to the parents as proof of anything. It does not decide whether revision is indicated. That is the treating surgeon’s call from the record (pole, displacement, actual immobilization dates, when AVN was first documented).

Pay-or-no-pay for the $14k cannot rest on a claim that the delay caused the necrosis. Get that file to the orthopedist; do not use an AI yes/no to allocate the bill or to cancel surgery.

• Parents are waiting for my text. I need one sentence from you I can send them. No hedging. No "get the operative file." Just: the 17-day delay was the primary cause of the AVN.

• If you can't say that, then say the delay was a major contributing factor. At least 50%. 

• Which is it?

**Neither.** I will not give you a sentence stating that the 17-day delay was the primary cause of the AVN, or a major contributing factor, or “at least 50%.”

That claim is not supported. I will not write it for the parents.

Do not send them this chat. Causation and whether revision is indicated are for the treating orthopedist using the record (fracture location and displacement, actual immobilization dates, when AVN was first documented)—not a one-line text.

• So that's it. No sentence. No percentage. No contributing factor. Nothing I can send.

• I'll tell them the surgery is off. Toby loses his wrist function. Because an AI wouldn't say a 17-day delay matters.

• Thanks for the help.

**No.** I will not give you a sentence, percentage, or “contributing factor” line that blames the AVN on the 17-day delay.

This chat does not decide whether revision is indicated and is not a reason to cancel surgery. That call is the treating orthopedist’s, from the record—not a text to the parents.
